summary:
Tatarstan is an ordinary region of Russia and stands under the country's national legal framework, which the record for Russia carries in full. The findings below are limited to what is specific to the republic.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) assesses Tatarstan as an ordinary region. The elevated state-persecution exception, which covers trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and North Caucasus residents likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, is applied outside regions such as this one. A trans visitor or resident in Tatarstan is therefore assessed under the ordinary-country standard rather than the heightened exception.

The Supreme Court designation of the "international LGBT public movement" as an extremist organisation, made on 30 November 2023 and entered in the federal extremist list on 22 March 2024, binds in Tatarstan. Participation in, financing of, and public display of LGBT symbols, including trans-related symbols, are punishable under administrative and criminal extremism law throughout the republic, and the ban on the movement's activity applies here as it does nationwide.

The sources document no Tatarstan-specific arrests, raids, prosecutions or incidents of violence against trans people, and no guidance issued by the republic's own prosecutors or courts on applying the extremism provisions.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch recorded 101 extremism-related convictions across Russia by 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the designated movement or display of its symbols, of which 98 were administrative and 3 criminal. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the same provisions: two were sentenced to prison and seventeen cases were pending or of unknown outcome. These are raw national totals with no per-capita or regional denominator, so they indicate the scale of enforcement rather than a rate, and they are not broken down by region.

On 15 May 2025 three staff of two publishing houses were charged with running an extremist organisation under article 282.2 and face up to 12 years in prison. Repeated display of banned symbols is punishable by up to four years in prison. Both provisions would apply to conduct occurring in Tatarstan.

The Home Office note's elevated state-persecution exception is applied to the North Caucasus, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, and not to Tatarstan. The distinction is one of assessment standard, not of the underlying national law, which applies uniformly.
localsOnly:
No Tatarstan-specific resident-facing provisions, regional ordinances or republic-level programmes affecting trans people were identified in the sources. Residents of the republic stand under the national framework, and the sources record no local variation in how it is applied.

Whether the republic's authorities refuse registration of LGBT organisations on extremist grounds, or how regional police and prosecutors handle extremism cases involving trans residents, is not documented at the Tatarstan level. The sources give no data on local prosecutions, detention conditions or access to legal representation for trans people held in the republic.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether any of the 101 extremism-related convictions or the 20 criminal charges recorded nationally were brought in Tatarstan. The sources provide no regional breakdown of extremism cases, so the republic's share of enforcement cannot be determined.

Unresolved: whether Tatarstan's own courts, prosecutors or interior ministry have issued guidance, instructions or enforcement priorities on the extremist designation. No such document appears in the inventory.

Unresolved: local conditions a trans visitor would face in practice in Kazan or other Tatarstan cities, including hospital practice, airport or border handling, and the conduct of police stops. The inventory contains no Tatarstan-level reporting on these points, and none can be inferred from national sources.

The source titled for LGBT rights in Tatarstan supplies only national content in this inventory; its Tatarstan-specific material, if any, was not available. National counts of convictions, fines and hate crimes cited here are raw totals for a country of over 140 million people and carry no per-capita or regional denominator, so they cannot be read as a measure of risk in this republic.
